stops.name: The broken path, vinegar and fire
stops.campa: The descent is worse than the climb: the track falls away where a landslide has carried the mountainside off, and the army stands stopped above a precipice of new snow over old ice. Hannibal sets them to build. They fell the great trees and raise a pyre against the living rock; when the stone is furnace-hot they pour their ration of sour wine into it, and the boulder splits with a crack like the mountain's own bone breaking. Iron finishes what fire began; hairpins are cut into the cliff; in one day there is a road for mules, in three for elephants. Livy carries the story; the register carries Livy.

stops.name: The plains of the Taurini, the counting of the remnant
stops.campa: Fifteen days in the Alps; five months from New Carthage. On the grass of the Po valley he counts what the mountains have left him: twenty thousand foot, six thousand horse: the army halved, the survivors more like ghosts than men, the horses skeletal. The numbers are not rumor: Hannibal himself will engrave them in bronze at the temple of Hera on Cape Lacinium, and Polybius will read them there with his own eyes. With this remnant he proposes to break the greatest power in the world. He lets them eat, and the flesh comes back onto man and horse, and the ghosts become an army.

stops.name: Taurini (Turin), the first lesson
stops.campa: The Taurini, at war with his would-be Gallic allies, decline his friendship. Their chief town holds three days; then it is taken, and everyone who bore arms in it is killed. It is not rage but arithmetic: the terror runs down the Po faster than any rider, and the wavering Gauls begin to come in. Before the walls he had paraded his Alpine captives and made them fight in pairs for freedom and a horse, so the army could watch its own condition made flesh: conquer, or die; there is no road back over the mountains.

stops.name: The Ticinus: first blood, and the boy Scipio
stops.campa: On the plain west of the Ticinus the horse of Carthage meets the horse of Rome, consul against general, and the Numidians fold around the Roman wings like water. The consul Publius Scipio goes down wounded in the press, and is cut free by a boy of seventeen who spurs in alone where his escort will not follow: his son, Publius Cornelius Scipio, one day to be called Africanus. The war's end rides onto the field at the war's first hour, and saves the life that will engender Zama. Rome retreats behind the Po by night, breaking the bridge.

stops.name: The Trebia, the ambush at the solstice
stops.campa: Snow and sleet at the winter solstice. Before dawn his Numidians bait the consul Sempronius across the Trebia: the Romans breakfastless, breast-deep in water running with ice. Hannibal's men have eaten by their fires and oiled themselves like athletes. In the streambed where the plain looks flat and hides everything, his brother Mago crouches with a thousand foot and a thousand horse, picked man by man. When the lines lock, Mago rises out of the earth at the Roman back. Elephants, cold, Numidians, ambush: the army of Rome breaks. Afterward the rains kill nearly every elephant, and the general goes on without them.

stops.name: Winter among the Gauls, the man of many wigs
stops.campa: He winters among allies he does not trust. The Gallic chiefs, tired of a war eating their own fields, are known to weigh his murder; so Hannibal has wigs made, and clothes to match each one, now a greybeard, now a man in his prime, now a young dandy, changing them so constantly that not only strangers but his own friends pass him in the camp lanes without knowing him. The assassins can find no fixed man to kill. All winter the deadliest soldier alive walks his own camp as a rumor.

stops.name: The Apennine ridge, beaten back by the storm
stops.campa: He tries the Apennines too early, and the mountain answers with a tempest the canon says was worse than anything in the Alps: rain driven level into the faces of the men, then hail, wind that tears every tent from its pegs, cold that kills. For once Hannibal turns back. The army shelters in the plain; more elephants die: after this only one remains alive, the great beast called Surus, the Syrian. Even the register of wonders records plainly: the weather defeated him where Rome had not.

stops.name: The marshes of the Arno, the eye given to Italy
stops.campa: To appear where no army can be, he takes the army where no army should go: four days and three nights through the flooded Arno country without dry ground to sleep on. Men doze on the packs of dead mules heaped in the water; the Gauls, marching in the churned middle of the column, sicken and despair; the Spaniards and Africans walk through on the firm bottom the unspoiled front provides. Hannibal rides the last elephant, Surus, above the fever-water, but the marsh takes its toll of him too: ophthalmia burns through his right eye. He comes out of the water half-blind and entirely unannounced, between Flaminius and Rome.

stops.name: Faesulae and the burning of Etruria, the baiting of Flaminius
stops.campa: Past Faesulae he turns the army loose on the richest country in Italy and burns it methodically, in sight of the consul's camp: smoke as a letter addressed to Flaminius personally. The consul is proud, popular, impatient of advice; Hannibal has studied him the way he studies ground. Omens pile up around the Roman: the consul's horse throws him, a standard cannot be pulled from the earth. Flaminius orders it dug out and follows the smoke. The trap he is walking toward is a lake shore shaped like a noose.

stops.name: Lake Trasimene, the battle in the fog
stops.campa: Mist off the lake fills the defile, and inside it waits the whole Carthaginian army, laid along the heights overnight. Flaminius marches his column in unscouted, and the hills come down on it from three sides with the lake as the fourth. Three hours of killing, so absorbed that a great earthquake passes through the battlefield unfelt. Ducarius the Insubrian knows the consul's face and drives his lance home; fifteen thousand die; the lake margins run red. Hannibal searches for Flaminius's body to bury it with honor; it is never found. Nineteen centuries on, Goethe will skirt this shore southward, in love with the Italy Hannibal holds by the throat.

stops.name: Spoletium, the gate that will be called Flight
stops.campa: He probes south from the lake and is thrown back bloodily from the gates of Spoletium, a single Latin colony holding like a knot in wood. Hannibal reads the repulse as a measurement: if one colony costs this much, what is the price of Rome? He turns east for the Adriatic instead. The town will name a gate Porta della Fuga, the Gate of Flight, and keep the name for two thousand years. Goethe will stand in Spoleto one October marveling at the aqueduct; the town he marvels at is the town that said no.

stops.name: Picenum, the horses bathed in old wine
stops.campa: On the Adriatic coast, in country fat with grain and orchards, he rests the army and repairs it like a smith repairing tools. The men eat until the marsh-sickness leaves them. The horses, mangy and worn to rope, he orders bathed in old wine, a prescription the canon records exactly, and their coats come back glossy under the Punic grooms' hands. Here too he re-arms his Libyans with captured Roman weapons, so that Africa now marches in Rome's own iron. From this shore he sends word by sea to Carthage for the first time since Spain: a letter of victories.
